content.paragraph: Among the many applications of integral calculus to physics and engineering, we consider two here: force due to water pressure and centers of mass. As with our previous applications to geometry (areas, volumes, and lengths) and to work, our strategy is to break up the physical quantity into a large number of small parts, approximate each small part, add the results (giving a Riemann sum), take the limit, and then evaluate the resulting integral.

subsection.title: Hydrostatic Pressure and Force
subsection.paragraph: Deep-sea divers know first-hand that water pressure increases as they dive deeper. This is because the weight of the water above them increases.

In general, suppose that a thin horizontal plate with area $$A$$ square meters is submerged in a fluid of density $$\rho$$ kilograms per cubic meter at a depth $$d$$ meters below the surface of the fluid as in Figure 1. The fluid directly above the plate (think of a column of liquid) has volume $$V = Ad$$ , so its mass is $$m = \rho V = \rho Ad$$ . The force exerted by the fluid on the plate is therefore
where $$g$$ is the acceleration due to gravity. The pressure $$P$$ on the plate is defined to be the force per unit area:

figure.alt_text: A horizontal and approximately square shaped area, labeled A, immersed in a fluid at a depth d from its surface.

subsection.paragraph: The SI unit for measuring pressure is a newton per square meter, which is called a pascal (abbreviation: $$1N/m^{2} = 1{Pa}$$ ). Since this is a small unit, the kilopascal (kPa) is often used. For instance, because the density of water is $$\rho = 1000{kg}/m^{3}$$ , the pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool $$2$$ m deep is

When using US Customary units, we write $$P = \rho gd = \delta d$$ , where $$\delta = \rho g$$ is the weight density (as opposed to $$\rho$$ , which is the mass density). For instance, the weight density of water is $$\delta = 62.5{lb}/{ft}^{3}$$ , so the pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool $$8{ft}$$ deep is $$P = \delta d = 62.5{lb}/{ft}^{3} \times 8{ft} = 500{lb}/{ft}^{2}$$ .

An important principle of fluid pressure is the experimentally verified fact that at any point in a liquid the pressure is the same in all directions. (A diver feels the same pressure on nose and both ears.) Thus the pressure in any direction at a depth $$d$$ in a fluid with mass density $$\rho$$ is given by

This helps us determine the hydrostatic force (the force exerted by a fluid at rest) against a vertical plate or wall or dam. This is not a straightforward problem because the pressure is not constant but increases as the depth increases.

subsection.paragraph: Next we consider a flat plate (called a lamina) with uniform density $$\rho$$ that occupies a region $$\mathcal{R}$$ of the plane. We wish to locate the center of mass of the plate, which is called the centroid of $$\mathcal{R}$$ . In doing so we use the following physical principles: the symmetry principle says that if $$\mathcal{R}$$ is symmetric about a line $$l$$ , then the centroid of $$\mathcal{R}$$ lies on $$l$$ . (If $$\mathcal{R}$$ is reflected about $$l$$ , then $$\mathcal{R}$$ remains the same so its centroid remains fixed. But the only fixed points lie on $$l$$ .) Thus the centroid of a rectangle is its center. Moments should be defined so that if the entire mass of a region is concentrated at the center of mass, then its moments remain unchanged. Also, the moment of the union of two nonoverlapping regions should be the sum of the moments of the individual regions.

Suppose that the region $$\mathcal{R}$$ is of the type shown in Figure 10(a); that is, $$\mathcal{R}$$ lies between the lines $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ , above the $$x$$-axis, and beneath the graph of $$f$$ , where $$f$$ is a continuous function. We divide the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ into $$n$$ subintervals with endpoints $$x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}$$ and equal width $$\Delta x$$ . We choose the sample point $$x_{i}^{*}$$ to be the midpoint $${\overline{x}}_{i}$$ of the $$i$$ th subinterval, that is, $${\overline{x}}_{i} = \left( x_{i - 1} + x_{i} \right)/2$$ . This determines the approximation to $$\mathcal{R}$$ by rectangles shown in Figure 10(b). The centroid of the $$i$$ th approximating rectangle $$R_{i}$$ is its center $$C_{i}{‍\left( {{\overline{x}}_{i},\frac{1}{2}f\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right)} \right)}$$ . Its area is $$f\left( {\overline{x}}_{i} \right)\Delta x$$ , so its mass is density × area:

problem.paragraph: Find the center of mass of a semicircular plate of radius $$r$$ with uniform density.

Solution In order to use (8) we place the semicircle as in Figure 11 so that $$f(x) = \sqrt{r^{2} - x^{2}}$$ and $$a = - r$$ , $$b = r$$ . Here there is no need to use the formula to calculate $$\overline{x}$$ because, by the symmetry principle, the center of mass must lie on the $$y$$-axis, so $$\overline{x} = 0$$ . The area of the semicircle is $$A = \frac{1}{2}\pi r^{2}$$ , so

paragraph.math: $$\begin{array}{l} {\overline{y} = \frac{1}{A}{\int_{- r}^{r}{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{2}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\pi r^{2}} \cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int_{- r}^{r}{\left( \sqrt{r^{2} - x^{2}} \right)^{2}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{2}{\pi r^{2}}{\int_{0}^{r}{(r^{2} - x^{2})dx}}\qquad({since\ the\ integrand\ is\ even})} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{2}{\pi r^{2}}\left\lbrack {r^{2}x - \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{r}} \\ {\phantom{\overline{y}} = \frac{2}{\pi r^{2}}\frac{2r^{3}}{3} = \frac{4r}{3\pi}} \end{array}$$

subsection.title: Theorem of Pappus
subsection.paragraph: We end this section by showing a surprising connection between centroids and volumes of revolution.

note.title: Theorem of Pappus
note.paragraph: Let $$\mathcal{R}$$ be a plane region that lies entirely on one side of a line $$l$$ in the plane. If $$\mathcal{R}$$ is rotated about $$l$$ , then the volume of the resulting solid is the product of the area $$A$$ of $$\mathcal{R}$$ and the distance $$d$$ traveled by the centroid of $$\mathcal{R}$$ .

statement.paragraph: Centroid of a Curve The centroid of a curve can be found by a process similar to the one we used for finding the centroid of a region. If $$C$$ is a curve with length $$L$$ , then the centroid is $$\left( {\overline{x},\overline{y}} \right)$$ where $$\overline{x} = (1/L)\int xds$$ and $$\overline{y} = (1/L)\int yds$$ . Here we assign appropriate limits of integration, and $$ds$$ is as defined in Sections 8.1 and 8.2. (The centroid often doesn’t lie on the curve itself. If the curve were made of wire and placed on a weightless board, the centroid would be the balance point on the board.) Find the centroid of the quarter-circle $$y = \sqrt{16 - x^{2}},0 \leqslant x \leqslant 4$$ .

exercise_group.instructions: 48–49 The Second Theorem of Pappus The Second Theorem of Pappus is in the same spirit as Pappus’s Theorem discussed in this section, but for surface area rather than volume: let $$C$$ be a curve that lies entirely on one side of a line $$l$$ in the plane. If $$C$$ is rotated about $$l$$ , then the area of the resulting surface is the product of the arc length of $$C$$ and the distance traveled by the centroid of $$C$$ (see Exercise 47).

subsection.title: Discovery Project Complementary Coffee Cups
subsection.paragraph: Suppose you have a choice of two coffee cups of the type shown, one that bends outward and one inward, and you notice that they have the same height and their shapes fit together snugly. You wonder which cup holds more coffee. Of course you could fill one cup with water and pour it into the other one but, being a calculus student, you decide on a more mathematical approach. Ignoring the handles, you observe that both cups are surfaces of revolution, so you can think of the coffee as a volume of revolution.

figure.alt_text: The figure has two parts. The first part is a three dimensional rendering of two cups, placed close together such that their sides touch. The cup on the left, labeled Cup A, resembles a cylinder with its sides bulging outward. The cup on the right, labeled Cup B, has sides that cave inward and its inward bulge overlaps the outward bulge of the cup A. The second part of the figure shows a curve, two lines, and two shaded regions graphed on the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The x axis has a single tick mark labeled k. The y axis has a single mark labeled h. The curve, labeled x = f(y), starts at the top, and goes down bulging rightward, until it meets the x axis at a point to the left of k. From k, a vertical line rises upward. From h, a horizontal line segment extends rightward brushing past the starting point of the curve, until it reaches the line x = k, thus creating a rectangle. The area of the rectangle on the left and the right of the curve are shaded with different colors. A curved arrow centered on the y axis points clockwise. A curved arrow centered on the line x = k points counterclockwise.
